claim: Optic flow plays an essential role in speed determination in insects.
source: Although optic flow plays an essential role in speed determination, it is less reliable under conditions of low light or sparse landmarks.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: Optic flow is less reliable under conditions of low light or sparse landmarks.
source: Although optic flow plays an essential role in speed determination, it is less reliable under conditions of low light or sparse landmarks.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Under conditions of low light or sparse landmarks, insects rely on feedback from antennal mechanosensors.
source: Under such conditions, insects rely on feedback from antennal mechanosensors but it is not clear how these inputs combine to elicit flight-related antennal behaviours.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Antennal movements of the honeybee, Apis mellifera, are governed by combined visual and antennal mechanosensory inputs.
source: We here show that antennal movements of the honeybee, Apis mellifera, are governed by combined visual and antennal mechanosensory inputs.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-4.

claim: Frontal airflow causes antennae to actively move forward as a sigmoidal function of absolute airspeed values.
source: Frontal airflow, as experienced during forward flight, causes antennae to actively move forward as a sigmoidal function of absolute airspeed values.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, D, E.

claim: Front-to-back optic flow causes antennae to move backward as a linear function of relative optic flow.
source: However, corresponding front-to-back optic flow causes antennae to move backward, as a linear function of relative optic flow, opposite the airspeed response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When combined, airflow and optic flow inputs maintain antennal position in a state of dynamic equilibrium.
source: When combined, these inputs maintain antennal position in a state of dynamic equilibrium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Purely optic flow-based measurements of self-motion can be misleading for insects which experience sideslip while flying in a crosswind.
source: For instance, purely optic flow-based measurements of self-motion can be misleading for insects which experience sideslip while flying in a crosswind.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about the limitations of single-modality sensing.

claim: Reliance on optic flow may be problematic under dimly lit or overcast conditions, or when flying over lakes or deserts which present sparse visual feedback.
source: Moreover, reliance on optic flow may be problematic under dimly lit or overcast conditions, or when flying over lakes or deserts which present sparse visual feedback.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about environmental conditions affecting optic flow reliability.

claim: Sampling from multiple sensory cues reduces the ambiguity arising from variability in feedback from single modalities.
source: In such situations, sampling from multiple sensory cues reduces the ambiguity arising from variability in feedback from single modalities (Wehner, 2003; Sherman and Dickinson, 2004; Wasserman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The integration of multimodal sensory cues is essential for most natural locomotory behaviours, including insect flight manoeuvres.
source: Hence, the integration of multimodal sensory cues is essential for most natural locomotory behaviours, including insect flight manoeuvres (Willis and Arbas, 1991; Frye et al., 2003; Verspui and Gray, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The importance of optic flow cues detected by compound eyes is well-documented in diverse insects, including honeybees.
source: For flight control, the importance of optic flow cues detected by compound eyes is well-documented in diverse insects, including honeybees (Srinivasan et al., 1996; Baird et al., 2005), bumblebees (Baird et al., 2010; Dyhr and Higgins, 2010), Megalopta (Baird et al., 2011) and Drosophila (David, 1982; Duistermars et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback from antennae has emerged as a key sensory input for insect flight.
source: In recent years, mechanosensory feedback from antennae has also emerged as a key sensory input for insect flight (Sane et al., 2007; Yorozu et al., 2009; Krishnan et al., 2012; Fuller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Antennal mechanosensory feedback is transduced primarily by two sets of mechanosensors: the chordotonal Johnston's organ (JO) and the antennal hair plates (or Böhm's bristles).
source: This feedback is transduced primarily by two sets of mechanosensors - the chordotonal Johnston's organ (JO) (Gewecke, 1974) which senses a wide range of stimuli from high-frequency antennal vibrations to low-frequency ambient airflow or gravity (Yorozu et al., 2009; Dieudonné et al., 2014), and the antennal hair plates (or Böhm's bristles) which are involved in the reflexive positioning of antennae during flight (Krishnan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Johnston's organ senses a wide range of stimuli from high-frequency antennal vibrations to low-frequency ambient airflow or gravity.
source: This feedback is transduced primarily by two sets of mechanosensors - the chordotonal Johnston's organ (JO) (Gewecke, 1974) which senses a wide range of stimuli from high-frequency antennal vibrations to low-frequency ambient airflow or gravity (Yorozu et al., 2009; Dieudonné et al., 2014), and the antennal hair plates (or Böhm's bristles) which are involved in the reflexive positioning of antennae during flight (Krishnan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Antennal hair plates (or Böhm's bristles) are involved in the reflexive positioning of antennae during flight.
source: This feedback is transduced primarily by two sets of mechanosensors - the chordotonal Johnston's organ (JO) (Gewecke, 1974) which senses a wide range of stimuli from high-frequency antennal vibrations to low-frequency ambient airflow or gravity (Yorozu et al., 2009; Dieudonné et al., 2014), and the antennal hair plates (or Böhm's bristles) which are involved in the reflexive positioning of antennae during flight (Krishnan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The characteristic positioning of the antennae at the onset of flight is ubiquitous in most, if not all, flying insects.
source: The characteristic positioning of the antennae at the onset of flight is ubiquitous in most, if not all, flying insects underscoring the evolutionary significance of its function (Dorsett, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of antennal positioning due to Böhm's bristle ablation or reduction of JO inputs severely impairs flight.
source: Disruption of antennal positioning due to Böhm's bristle ablation or reduction of JO inputs severely impairs flight (Willis et al., 1995; Hinterwirth and Daniel, 2010; Sane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The control of antennal position is thought to be essential for the unambiguous sensing of inputs by the JO.
source: The control of antennal position is thought to be essential for the unambiguous sensing of inputs by the JO (Hinterwirth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When tethered bees are presented with fixed airflow but no optic flow, they hold their antennae at constant IAA throughout a flight bout.
source: When presented with fixed airflow but no optic flow, both tethered and freely-flying bees held their antennae at constant IAA throughout a flight bout (e.g. Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: As frontal airflow increased, both antennae moved forward and mean IAA at each airflow value decreased as a sigmoidal function of airspeed in both tethered and freely-flying bees.
source: As frontal airflow increased, both antennae moved forward and mean IAA at each airflow value decreased as a sigmoidal function of airspeed (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The linear region of the sigmoid IAA response to airspeed lay between 1.5 to 3 m/s.
source: The linear region of the sigmoid lay between 1.5 to 3 m/s (grey bar, Figure 1C,D), changing by approximately 35o (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) in tethered and 25° (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) in freely-flying bees, significantly decreasing with each step change in airspeed (step change = 0.5 m/s; *p<0.0001; Moore's paired test; N=10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, D and statistical analysis.

claim: IAA changed by approximately 35° in tethered bees in the linear region of the sigmoid response.
source: The linear region of the sigmoid lay between 1.5 to 3 m/s (grey bar, Figure 1C,D), changing by approximately 35o (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) in tethered and 25° (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) in freely-flying bees, significantly decreasing with each step change in airspeed (step change = 0.5 m/s; *p<0.0001; Moore's paired test; N=10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IAA changed by approximately 25° in freely-flying bees in the linear region of the sigmoid response.
source: The linear region of the sigmoid lay between 1.5 to 3 m/s (grey bar, Figure 1C,D), changing by approximately 35o (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) in tethered and 25° (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) in freely-flying bees, significantly decreasing with each step change in airspeed (step change = 0.5 m/s; *p<0.0001; Moore's paired test; N=10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Antennal behaviour was similar regardless of whether airspeed stimulus was presented in linearly increasing or decreasing steps or in random order.
source: This behaviour was similar regardless of whether airspeed stimulus was presented in linearly increasing or decreasing steps (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) or in random order (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C, E and supplements.

claim: Antennal position is calibrated against absolute airspeeds, independent of time history.
source: Thus, antennal position is calibrated against absolute airspeeds, independent of time history.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar responses to randomized and sequential airspeed presentations.

claim: At airspeeds less than 1.5 m/s or greater than 3 m/s, mean IAA at each airflow plateaued in both tethered and freely-flying bees.
source: At airspeeds less than 1.5 m/s or greater than 3 m/s, mean IAA at each airflow plateaued in both tethered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) and freely-flying bees (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C, D.

claim: As frontal airflow in the wind tunnel increased, freely-flying honeybees modulated their flight to maintain roughly constant groundspeed of ca. 0.4 m/s.
source: As frontal airflow in the wind tunnel increased, freely-flying honeybees modulated their flight to maintain roughly constant groundspeed of ca. 0.4 m/s (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; also [Barron and Srinivasan, 2006]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and citation to previous literature.

claim: In freely-flying bees, there was no correlation between groundspeed and IAA.
source: In these bees, we observed no correlation between groundspeed and IAA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Bees with restricted JO positioned their antennae at the onset of flight but their mean IAA at each airflow was insensitive to changing airspeeds.
source: Unlike sham-treated bees which showed the typical sigmoid response to frontal airflow (Figure 1F, non-normalized data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, N=5), bees with restricted JO positioned their antennae at the onset of flight (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I; also [Krishnan et al., 2012]) but their mean IAA at each airflow was insensitive to changing airspeeds (Figure 1G, N=7; p>0.1, Moore's paired test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and statistical analysis.

claim: JO input is required for antennal positioning during flight, but not at flight onset.
source: These experiments established that JO input is required for antennal positioning during flight, but not at flight onset (Krishnan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on JO-restricted bees and supported by citation.

claim: The antennal positioning at flight onset is a separate process from the inflight modulation of IAA.
source: Thus, the antennal positioning at flight onset is a separate process from the inflight modulation of IAA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing JO-restricted bees can position antennae at flight onset but not modulate them during flight.

claim: Visual feedback is critical for regulation of groundspeed and height, or in centring trajectories through narrow corridors in diverse flying insects.
source: For example, visual feedback is critical for regulation of groundspeed and height, or in centring trajectories through narrow corridors in diverse flying insects (bees: [Srinivasan et al., 1996; Baird et al., 2005], Drosophila: [Straw et al., 2010], moths: [Kuenen and Baker, 1982], review: [Collett et al., 1993]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Visual feedback influences antennal position in insects that antennate during walking.
source: It also influences antennal position in insects that antennate during walking (Ye et al., 2003; Honegger, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies on optic flow dependent behaviours in honeybees have demonstrated that they extract angular velocity cues from the image motion, independent of spatial or temporal frequencies.
source: Note that, previous studies on optic flow dependent behaviours in honeybees have typically demonstrated that they extract angular velocity (ratio of temporal and spatial frequency) cues from the image motion, independent of spatial (Srinivasan et al., 1991) or temporal frequencies (Baird et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When temporal frequency increased from 0 to 25 cps, an initial sharp adjustment in IAA was followed by a graded response between 0 to approx. 10 cps, beyond which the value reached a plateau.
source: When temporal frequency increased from 0 to 25 cps, an initial sharp adjustment in IAA (red curve, Figure 2B, summary figure Figure 2F) was followed by a graded response between 0 to approx. 10 cps (grey bar, Figure 2B), beyond which the value reached a plateau.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2F.

claim: The response curve for linearly decreasing optic flow (25 to 0 cps) was similar to the increasing cues, except for the lack of initial sharp IAA adjustment from zero to non-zero optic flow.
source: The response curve for linearly decreasing optic flow (25 to 0 cps, green curve, Figure 2B, summary figure Figure 2G) was similar to the increasing cues, except for the lack of initial sharp IAA adjustment from zero to non-zero optic flow (also Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, 2G and supplements.

claim: Bees respond to changes in temporal frequency rather than their absolute value.
source: Thus, our data show that antennomotor activity in honey bees tracks changes in temporal frequency, and not their absolute value.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing responses to randomized optic flow presentations.

claim: Bee antennae robustly tracked simple sinusoidal stimuli that were both, cycled between front-to-back (0 to 1.8 cps), and back-to-front grating movement (0 to -1.8 to 0 cps) over the 10 s duration.
source: For example, bee antennae robustly tracked simple sinusoidal stimuli that were both, cycled between front-to-back (0 to 1.8 cps), and back-to-front grating movement (0 to -1.8 to 0 cps) over the 10 s duration (Figure 2H), thus verifying that the antennae move in both directions as a function of optic flow.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: All bees increased their IAA as a function of optic flow in the range 0-1.8 cps, with each step change of 0.3 cps eliciting significant increase in mean IAA.
source: Despite inter-animal variability in the set points for IAA at zero optic flow (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), all bees increased their IAA as a function of optic flow (Figure 2I), with each step change of 0.3 cps eliciting significant increase in mean IAA (*p<0.0001; Moore's paired test, N=10) at that optic flow rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I and statistical analysis.

claim: The IAA response of tethered bees to optic flow remained intact even when their JO were restricted by gluing the pedicel-flagellar joint.
source: The IAA response of tethered bees to optic flow remained intact (Figure 2J; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) even when their JO were restricted by gluing the pedicel-flagellar joint, establishing that it is independent of the JO pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Front-to-back optic flow causes antenna to move backward, opposite to frontal airflow which causes antenna to move actively forward.
source: Thus, front-to-back optic flow causes antenna to move backward, opposite to frontal airflow which causes antenna to move actively forward.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing opposite effects of airflow and optic flow on IAA.

claim: The JO-based antennal mechanosensory feedback was calibrated against absolute values of airspeed.
source: Whereas the JO-based antennal mechanosensory feedback was calibrated against absolute values of airspeed, visual feedback was calibrated relative to changes in optic flow under or across a threshold value.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing responses to airspeed and optic flow.

claim: Visual feedback was calibrated relative to changes in optic flow under or across a threshold value.
source: Whereas the JO-based antennal mechanosensory feedback was calibrated against absolute values of airspeed, visual feedback was calibrated relative to changes in optic flow under or across a threshold value.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing responses to optic flow.

claim: Antennae maintained position when the cue combination changed from Regime B to Regime A.
source: Antennae maintained position when the cue combination changed from Regime B to Regime A (green line; Figure 3B; Pp>0.1, Moore's test), but not when only airflow or optic flow was changed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis.

claim: When airspeed alone decreased from 2.5 to 0.5 m/s, both antennae moved backward.
source: When airspeed alone (i.e. with static grating) decreased from 2.5 to 0.5 m/s (blue line; Figure 3B; p<0.001, Moore's test), both antennae moved backward.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis.

claim: Antennae moved forward when optic flow alone decreased from 0.9 to 0.3 cps.
source: However, they moved forward when optic flow alone (i.e. with fan off) decreased from 0.9 to 0.3 cps (red line; Figure 3B; p<0.001; Moore's test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis.

claim: When the cue combination changed from Regime B to Regime C, antennae maintained position.
source: Similarly, when the cue combination changed from Regime B to Regime C, antennae again maintained position (green line; Figure 3C; p>0.1, Moore's test), but moved forward when airflow alone increased from 2.5 to 4 m/s (blue line; Figure 3C) and backward when optic flow alone increased from 0.9 to 1.8 cps (red line; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and statistical analysis.

claim: Visual and airflow cues elicit opposite IAA responses which, when acting in concert, maintain antennal position.
source: Thus, visual and airflow cues elicit opposite IAA responses which, when acting in concert, maintain antennal position.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing opposite effects that cancel when combined.

claim: When both airflow and optic flow cues were co-varied, ΔIAA did not significantly change.
source: However, when both cues were co-varied, ΔIAA did not significantly change (green, Figure 3D,E; p>0.1, Moore's test) and their means were statistically indistinguishable from zero.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, E and statistical analysis.

claim: The IAA response curves to optic flow in presence of two constant values (0 and 1 m/s) of airspeed were uniformly offset over the range from 0 to 1.8 cps.
source: We measured IAA against optic flow in presence of two constant values (0 and 1 m/s) of airspeed. The two curves were uniformly offset over the range from 0 to 1.8 cps (compare dotted and solid lines, Figure 4A,B; *p<0.05, Moore's test, N=8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B and statistical analysis.

claim: For airspeeds between 0 and 4 m/s, a steady offset was observed for greater optic flow, but in the opposite direction.
source: Similarly, for airspeeds between 0 and 4 m/s, we observed a steady offset for greater optic flow, but in the opposite direction (compare dotted and solid lines, Figure 4C,D; *p<0.05, Moore's test, N=9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D and statistical analysis.

claim: The antennomotor system linearly combines the multimodal cues and recalibrates accordingly.
source: Thus, the antennomotor system linearly combines the multimodal cues and recalibrates accordingly.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing uniform offsets in response curves.

claim: Antennal hair plates are stimulated when the antenna undergoes a substantial movement in the scape-head capsule or pedicel-scape joints.
source: To summarize these studies: antennal hair plates are stimulated when the antenna undergoes a substantial movement in the scape-head capsule or pedicel-scape joints.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous studies.

claim: The mechanosensory neurons underlying antennal hair plates directly project into the Antennal Motor and Mechanosensory Center (AMMC) where they arborize on the dendritic fields of antennal motor neurons and activate them.
source: The mechanosensory neurons underlying these bristles directly project into the Antennal Motor and Mechanosensory Center (AMMC) where they arborize on the dendritic fields of antennal motor neurons and activate them.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous studies.

claim: Any gross change in antennal position elicits a rapid reflexive correction of the antennal position with latencies under 10 ms in hawk moths.
source: Any gross change in antennal position thus elicits a rapid reflexive correction of the antennal position with latencies under 10 ms in hawk moths (Krishnan et al., 2012) and probably on the same order in honeybees and other insects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and speculation about honeybees.

claim: The arrangement of the hair plates in different insects varies, but the underlying neural circuitry and hair plate function is conserved in moths, bees, and most other insect orders.
source: Although arrangement of the hair plates in different insects varies, the underlying neural circuitry and hair plate function is conserved in moths, bees, and most other insect orders (Krishnan and Sane, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The initial positioning of antennae at the flight onset (antennal deployment) is separate from its later inflight maintenance by the multimodal inputs (inflight antennal positioning).
source: Our study shows that the initial positioning of antennae at the flight onset (antennal deployment) is separate from its later inflight maintenance by the multimodal inputs (inflight antennal positioning).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on JO-restricted bees.

claim: Both antennal deployment and inflight antennal positioning behaviours require the hair plate-mediated reflex pathway.
source: Both behaviours require the hair plate-mediated reflex pathway but the set-point of this reflex system is under multimodal control in the latter case.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and previous studies.

claim: Restriction of the JO feedback has no effect on the antennal deployment behaviour, whereas it completely disrupts inflight antennal positioning.
source: In particular, restriction of the JO feedback has no effect on the antennal deployment behaviour, whereas it completely disrupts inflight antennal positioning.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on JO-restricted bees.

claim: Visual feedback drives the activity of both ipsi- and contralateral antennal motor neurons in moths.
source: Unlike the hair plate reflexes which are strictly unilateral (Krishnan et al., 2012), visual feedback drives the activity of both ipsi- and contralateral antennal motor neurons in moths (Krishnan and Sane, 2014) and may therefore serve to coordinate the movements of both antennae.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The integration of antennal mechanosensory and visual inputs mediates abdominal flexion in moths.
source: Recent studies have also described how the integration of antennal mechanosensory and visual inputs mediates abdominal flexion in moths (Hinterwirth and Daniel, 2010) which in turn is relevant for flight control and balance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In honeybees, the combined effect of antennal mechanosensory and visual inputs on the abdominal streamlining behaviour enables drag reduction during flight.
source: In honeybees too, their combined effect on the abdominal streamlining behaviour enables drag reduction during flight (Luu et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In freely-flying moths, the stimulation of antennal muscles elicits abdominal flexion accompanied by a change in flight trajectory.
source: In freely-flying moths, the stimulation of antennal muscles elicits abdominal flexion accompanied by a change in flight trajectory (Hinterwirth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Integration of mechanosensory and visual information mediates flight control in Drosophila.
source: Similarly, integration of mechanosensory and visual information mediates flight control in other insects such as Drosophila (Sherman and Dickinson, 2003; Fuller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The relative influence of mechanosensory input is greater during rapid turns, while visual input is more important during slower rotations.
source: Whereas the relative influence of mechanosensory input is greater during rapid turns, visual input is more important during slower rotations (Sherman and Dickinson, 2003; 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The integration of multimodal cues quite likely occurs in the Antennal Motor and Mechanosensory Centre (AMMC) region of the insect brain.
source: The integration of these multimodal cues quite likely occurs in the Antennal Motor and Mechanosensory Centre (AMMC) region of the insect brain, which houses the soma of the antennal motor neurons.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The AMMC region receives the arbors of motion-sensitive visual interneurons.
source: This region also receives the arbors of motion-sensitive visual interneurons (Hertel and Maronde, 1987), and likely also the inputs from cephalic hair mechano-afferents.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In locusts, the tritocerebral commissure giant (TCG) interneurone integrates visual and airflow information.
source: In locusts, the tritocerebral commissure giant (TCG) interneurone integrates visual and airflow information (Bacon and Tyrer, 1978), while other descending interneurons in crickets integrate antennal mechanosensory and visual inputs (Gebhardt and Honegger, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other descending interneurons in crickets integrate antennal mechanosensory and visual inputs.
source: In locusts, the tritocerebral commissure giant (TCG) interneurone integrates visual and airflow information (Bacon and Tyrer, 1978), while other descending interneurons in crickets integrate antennal mechanosensory and visual inputs (Gebhardt and Honegger, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IAA responds to absolute airspeed values from 1.5 to 3 m/s, which is narrow compared to the typical range of airspeeds (between 0 and 7 m/s) of honeybees in free flight.
source: A key finding of this paper is that IAA responds to absolute airspeed values from 1.5 to 3 m/s, which is narrow compared to the typical range of airspeeds (between 0 and 7 m/s; [Wenner, 1963])of honeybees in free flight.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous literature.

claim: The odometer in honeybees is visual.
source: As shown in studies over the past two decades, the odometer in honeybees is quite clearly visual (Srinivasan, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The visual system can extract the overall image motion, which is perceived by and integrated over the motion detectors in the retina.
source: The visual system can extract the overall image motion, which is perceived by and integrated over the motion detectors in the retina (Zanker et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Honeybees trained to find food at a specific distance in tunnels lined with visual stripes can correctly judge distances even when the spatial frequency of the stripes is altered.
source: Honeybees trained to find food at a specific distance in tunnels lined with visual stripes can correctly judge distances even when the spatial frequency of the stripes is altered (Baird et al., 2005; Srinivasan et al., 1996; 1997; 2000; 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Honeybees estimate distances correctly despite head or tailwinds, suggesting that parameters such as windspeed, flight duration and number of wing beats play no role in the odometry.
source: Moreover, they estimate distances correctly despite head or tailwinds, suggesting that parameters such as windspeed, flight duration and number of wing beats etc. play no role in the odometry.
evidence: This is supported by inference from previous literature.

claim: Image motion cues can be used to estimate depth and distinguish between near and far objects independent of their size.
source: Indeed, image motion cues can also be used to estimate depth and distinguish between near and far objects independent of their size (Kirchner and Srinivasan, 1989; Srinivasan et al., 1989; Zhang et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bees appear to be able to separately process size and velocity cues.
source: Thus, bees appear to be able to separately process size and velocity cues (Srinivasan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Honeybees are able to extract information about both airspeed and groundspeed.
source: Complement to the visual odometer, we show here that honeybees are also able to extract information about both airspeed and groundspeed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in this study.

claim: The airspeed calibration mediated by JO is absolute, but works over a narrow speed range.
source: Importantly, the airspeed calibration mediated by JO is absolute, but works over a narrow speed range, whereas the groundspeed calibration mediated by optic flow can be tuned over a broader range.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data in this study.

claim: The groundspeed calibration mediated by optic flow can be tuned over a broader range.
source: Importantly, the airspeed calibration mediated by JO is absolute, but works over a narrow speed range, whereas the groundspeed calibration mediated by optic flow can be tuned over a broader range.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data in this study.

claim: Honeybees calibrate their optic flow speedometer using their JO-based system that measures absolute airspeeds.
source: We propose the hypothesis that honeybees calibrate their optic flow speedometer using their JO-based system that measures absolute airspeeds (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: At the onset of a regular flight bout, bees simultaneously sample the optic flow and airspeed.
source: At the onset of a regular flight bout, bees simultaneously sample the optic flow (red lines) and airspeed (blue line).
evidence: This is part of the proposed hypothesis.

claim: Sampling the optic flow corresponding to the dynamic range of the JO-based airspeed sensor provides bees with the means to cross-calibrate average optic flow against absolute airspeeds.
source: Sampling the optic flow (Figure 4F; black segments on the red lines) corresponding to the dynamic range of the JO-based airspeed sensor (e.g. between ~1.5 to 3 m/s) provides bees with the means to cross-calibrate average optic flow against absolute airspeeds.
evidence: This is part of the proposed hypothesis.

claim: The optic flow-based speedometer requires extrapolation well beyond the range of the antennal system.
source: As the airspeed-based estimation only works in a narrow range from 1.5 to 3 m/s, the optic flow-based speedometer requires extrapolation well beyond the range of the antennal system.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the narrow range of airspeed sensing.

claim: A disadvantage of the proposed calibration system is that it must be recalibrated at the beginning of each bout, or within bouts in case of sudden gusts of wind which may confound the calibration.
source: A disadvantage of such a system is that it must be recalibrated at the beginning of each bout, or within bouts in case of sudden gusts of wind which may confound the calibration.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the proposed hypothesis.

claim: Under circumstances of sudden gusts of wind, honeybees would have to slow down to recalibrate their optic flow based speedometer against the airspeed-based speedometer, before resuming flight.
source: Under such circumstances, we predict that honeybees would have to slow down to recalibrate their optic flow based speedometer against the airspeed-based speedometer, before resuming flight.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed hypothesis.

claim: Honeybees freely flying within a tunnel lined with checkerboard patterns flew at speeds of approximately 0.4 m/s.
source: In their study on visual regulation of groundspeeds in honeybees, Barron and Srinivasan (Barron and Srinivasan, 2006) observed that honeybees freely flying within a tunnel lined with checkerboard patterns flew at speeds of approximately 0.4 m/s.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: When the checkerboard pattern was replaced by an axial-stripe pattern which offered sparse optic flow cues, honeybee groundspeed was maintained with low variance at a value of 1.4 m/s.
source: However, when the checkerboard pattern was replaced by an axial-stripe pattern which offered sparse optic flow cues, its groundspeed was maintained with low variance at a value of 1.4 m/s.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In absence of optic flow, the bees rely on their JO-based airflow sensors to both set and maintain groundspeed.
source: To explain this result, we propose that, in absence of optic flow, the bees rely on their JO-based airflow sensors to both set and maintain groundspeed.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for observations from previous literature.

claim: The value of 1.4 m/s lies at the cusp of the airflow response curve.
source: It is worth noting that the value of 1.4 m/s lies at the cusp of the airflow response curve (Figure 1C), and is maintained as the new reference at different wind speeds in sparse optic flow (see Figure 3 in Barron and Srinivasan [2006]).
evidence: This is an observation connecting current data with previous literature.

claim: The honeybee odometer follows the Weber's law.
source: One would expect such a speedometer system to accumulate errors as the range increases, as has also been observed with the honeybee odometer, which follows the Weber's law (Cheng et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: All experiments were performed on the European honeybees, Apis mellifera.
source: All experiments were performed on the European honeybees, Apis mellifera, maintained in an apiary in an outdoor insectary approximately 60 m from the lab.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: The digitization error was within 0.5%–1.5% for tethered bees and 3%–5% for freely flying bees.
source: The variation in antennal length in the digitized videos was used to estimate digitization error, which was within 0.5%–1.5% for tethered bees and 3%–5% for freely flying bees.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about measurement accuracy.
